the-forme-of-cury.name: The Forme of Cury
the-forme-of-cury.summary: Extensive 14th-century collection of medieval English recipes attributed to King Richard II's chief cooks; among the oldest English cookery books and the earliest to mention olive oil and certain spices.

richard-ii-of-england.name: Richard II of England
richard-ii-of-england.summary: King of England from 1377 until his deposition in 1399, who became king at age 10, suppressed the 1381 Peasants' Revolt, and cultivated a refined court centered on art and culture.

clarissa-dickson-wright.name: Clarissa Dickson Wright
clarissa-dickson-wright.summary: English celebrity cook, television personality and writer (1947–2014), best known as one of the Two Fat Ladies on the 1996–1999 cooking programme.

poume-d-oranges.name: Poume d'oranges
poume-d-oranges.summary: A gilded pork meatball dish of the medieval elite, made to resemble oranges with an egg yolk glaze and served at courtly English feasts, including Henry IV's coronation.

henry-iv-of-england.name: Henry IV of England
henry-iv-of-england.summary: King of England from 1399 to 1413 who deposed his cousin Richard II, founded the House of Lancaster's rule, and was the first English king whose native language was English.

eleanor-of-england-countess-of-leicester.name: Eleanor of England
eleanor-of-england-countess-of-leicester.summary: Youngest child of King John of England, who married Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester, and lived from 1215 to 1275.
eleanor-of-england-countess-of-leicester.source_title: Eleanor of England, Countess of Leicester

john-king-of-england.name: King John
john-king-of-england.summary: King of England from 1199 to 1216, nicknamed 'Lackland'; he lost Normandy to France, and the baronial revolt against him led to Magna Carta.

edward-i.name: Edward I
edward-i.summary: King of England from 1272 to 1307, called 'Hammer of the Scots,' who reformed royal administration and law after suppressing a baronial rebellion and joining the Ninth Crusade.

guillaume-tirel.name: Guillaume Tirel (Taillevent)
guillaume-tirel.summary: A cook to the French royal court around the time of the Hundred Years' War (c. 1310–1395), author of one of the earliest known French cookery books.

charles-v-of-france.name: Charles V of France
charles-v-of-france.summary: King of France from 1364 to 1380, called 'the Wise'; his armies recovered territory lost in the Hundred Years' War and he created France's first permanent paid army.

le-m-nagier-de-paris.name: Le Ménagier de Paris
le-m-nagier-de-paris.summary: A French guidebook from 1393 on a woman's proper conduct in marriage and running a household, including recipes and gardening tips, written as an elderly husband's advice.

le-de-france.name: Île-de-France
le-de-france.summary: The most populous region of France, containing Paris and often called the Paris Region; it holds about a fifth of France's population and nearly a third of its GDP.

picardy.name: Picardy
picardy.summary: A historical region of northern France first officially recognized in the 13th century, never established as a duchy or county, and now part of the Hauts-de-France region.

basilica-of-saint-denis.name: Abbey of Saint-Denis
basilica-of-saint-denis.summary: A former abbey church near Paris whose choir, completed in 1144, is considered the first fully Gothic structure; it became the burial place of nearly every French king from the 10th to 19th centuries.

gothic-architecture.name: Opus Francigenum
gothic-architecture.summary: The contemporary Latin name for what became known as Gothic architecture, meaning 'French work'; the term 'Gothic' was only applied later, contemptuously, during the Renaissance.

reims-cathedral.name: Reims Cathedral
reims-cathedral.summary: A Gothic cathedral in Reims, France, traditionally used for the coronation of French kings and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991.

chartres-cathedral.name: Chartres Cathedral
chartres-cathedral.summary: A Catholic cathedral near Paris built mostly between 1194 and 1220, considered a leading example of High Gothic architecture and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979.

amiens-cathedral.name: Amiens Cathedral
amiens-cathedral.summary: A Gothic cathedral in Amiens, France, built almost entirely between 1220 and 1270; it is the largest French cathedral by volume and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

flying-buttress.name: Flying buttress
flying-buttress.summary: An arching support that carries the outward-pushing forces of stone vaulted ceilings and roofs from a wall to a separate pier, without touching the wall at ground level like an ordinary buttress.

international-gothic.name: International Gothic
international-gothic.summary: A period of Gothic art beginning in Burgundy and northern Italy in the late 14th and early 15th centuries that spread across Western Europe, reducing variation in national artistic styles.

sens-cathedral.name: Sens Cathedral
sens-cathedral.summary: A cathedral in Sens, France, whose choir (begun 1135–1140, consecrated 1164) is considered the first built in the Gothic style, and whose builder later reconstructed Canterbury Cathedral's choir.

senlis-cathedral.name: Senlis Cathedral
senlis-cathedral.summary: A former Roman Catholic cathedral in Senlis, France, built mostly in the late 12th century in the early Gothic style, with a notable 13th-century south tower over 78 meters tall.

norwich-cathedral.name: Norwich Cathedral
norwich-cathedral.summary: A Church of England cathedral begun in 1096, largely Norman in structure, known for its ornate 15th-century vaulted ceiling and its 315-foot spire, the second tallest in England.

boss-architecture.name: Boss (architecture)
boss-architecture.summary: A decorative knob on a ceiling, wall or sculpture in architecture, or a raised prominence on cut stone.

saint-guilhem-le-d-sert.name: Saint-Guilhem-le-Désert
saint-guilhem-le-d-sert.summary: Medieval village in southern France, on the pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela, at the meeting of the Gellone valley and the Hérault gorge.

bayeux.name: Bayeux
bayeux.summary: A town in Normandy, France, home to the Bayeux Tapestry depicting the Norman Conquest, and the first major town liberated by the Allies after D-Day.

william-of-sens.name: William of Sens
william-of-sens.summary: 12th-century French master mason and architect (d. 1180) who rebuilt the choir of Canterbury Cathedral, an early example of Gothic style in England.

canterbury-cathedral.name: Canterbury Cathedral
canterbury-cathedral.summary: The cathedral of the archbishop of Canterbury and seat of the worldwide Anglican Communion, founded in 597 and rebuilt in Gothic style after a fire in 1174, largely to accommodate pilgrims visiting Thomas Becket's shrine.

worcester-cathedral.name: Worcester Cathedral
worcester-cathedral.summary: A Church of England cathedral in Worcester, founded in 680 and rebuilt from 1084 in the Romanesque style, later a pilgrimage site holding the shrines of St Wulfstan and St Oswald.

john-clyve.name: John Clyve
john-clyve.summary: English Gothic architect responsible for the nave, tower and west front of Worcester Cathedral, recorded as a mason there around 1376–77.

durham-cathedral.name: Durham Cathedral
durham-cathedral.summary: English cathedral holding the shrines of saints Cuthbert and Bede, with a Romanesque nave completed between 1093 and 1133 containing an early pointed rib vault.

lessay-abbey.name: Lessay Abbey
lessay-abbey.summary: An 11th-century Romanesque Benedictine abbey church in Normandy, France, notable as one of the earliest buildings to use rib vaulting, a technique later central to Gothic architecture.

wulfstan-died-1095.name: Wulfstan
wulfstan-died-1095.summary: English Benedictine monk and Bishop of Worcester from 1062 to 1095, the last surviving bishop from before the Norman Conquest, later venerated as a saint.

charles-viii-of-france.name: Charles VIII of France
charles-viii-of-france.summary: King of France from 1483 to 1498, called 'the Affable'; his marriage to Anne of Brittany brought Brittany into union with France, and he invaded Italy in 1494 with powerful new artillery.

giovanni-giocondo.name: Giovanni Giocondo (Fra Giocondo)
giovanni-giocondo.summary: Italian Franciscan friar, architect, antiquary and classical scholar (c. 1433–1515).

domenico-da-cortona.name: Domenico da Cortona
domenico-da-cortona.summary: Italian architect (about 1465 to about 1549), a pupil of Giuliano da Sangallo, brought to France by Charles VIII and credited with the design of the Château de Chambord.

ch-teau-d-amboise.name: Château d'Amboise
ch-teau-d-amboise.summary: A château in France's Loire Valley, confiscated by the French monarchy in the 15th century and rebuilt as a favored royal residence; King Charles VIII died there in 1498.

william-the-conqueror.name: William the Conqueror
william-the-conqueror.summary: First Norman king of England (r. 1066–1087) and Duke of Normandy, who defeated Harold Godwinson at Hastings and began the Norman Conquest.

harold-godwinson.name: Harold Godwinson
harold-godwinson.summary: Last crowned Anglo-Saxon king of England, reigning from January 1066 until his death at the Battle of Hastings that October, when he was defeated by William the Conqueror.

charles-vii-of-france.name: Charles VII of France
charles-vii-of-france.summary: King of France from 1422 to 1461, called 'the Victorious'; his reign saw the end of the Hundred Years' War, aided by the emergence of Joan of Arc.

compagnie-d-ordonnance.name: Compagnies d'ordonnance
compagnie-d-ordonnance.summary: The first standing army of late medieval and early modern France, built around heavily armoured cavalrymen with supporting archers and men-at-arms, established under Charles VII.

battle-of-poitiers.name: Battle of Poitiers
battle-of-poitiers.summary: A 19 September 1356 Hundred Years' War battle in which Edward the Black Prince's outnumbered Anglo-Gascon force defeated and captured France's King John II near Poitiers.

battle-of-formigny.name: Battle of Formigny
battle-of-formigny.summary: A decisive French victory over England on 15 April 1450 near the end of the Hundred Years' War, notable as one of the first European battles to use field artillery.

harald-hardrada.name: Harald Hardrada
harald-hardrada.summary: King of Norway from 1046 to 1066 who spent 15 years in exile as a mercenary, rising to command the Byzantine Varangian Guard before returning to claim his throne.

tostig-godwinson.name: Tostig Godwinson
tostig-godwinson.summary: Anglo-Saxon Earl of Northumbria and brother of King Harold Godwinson who, after being exiled, supported Harald Hardrada's invasion and died with him at Stamford Bridge in 1066.

battle-of-stamford-bridge.name: Battle of Stamford Bridge
battle-of-stamford-bridge.summary: A battle fought on 25 September 1066 in England, in which King Harold Godwinson defeated an invading Norwegian army, killing King Harald Hardrada and Tostig Godwinson; traditionally seen as marking the end of the Viking Age.

hundred-years-war-1337-1360.name: Edwardian War
hundred-years-war-1337-1360.summary: The first phase of the Hundred Years' War (1337-1360), begun when Edward III of England claimed the French throne; it ended with the Treaty of Brétigny confirming his rule over Aquitaine.

hundred-years-war-1369-1389.name: Caroline War
hundred-years-war-1369-1389.summary: The second phase of the Hundred Years' War (1369-1389), named for Charles V of France, who resumed fighting and largely reversed England's earlier territorial gains.

hundred-years-war-1415-1453.name: Lancastrian War
hundred-years-war-1415-1453.summary: The third and final phase of the Hundred Years' War (1415-1453), beginning with Henry V's invasion of Normandy and ending with England's defeat in Aquitaine.

john-talbot-1st-earl-of-shrewsbury.name: John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury
john-talbot-1st-earl-of-shrewsbury.summary: John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury: English military commander (c.1387–1453), the most feared English captain in France during the Hundred Years' War, killed leading an ill-advised charge against field artillery.

battle-of-castillon.name: Battle of Castillon
battle-of-castillon.summary: A 1453 battle in Gascony where French artillery destroyed an English force under John Talbot, ending English rule over nearly all of France and causing political instability in England.

gascony.name: Gascony
gascony.summary: A historic province of southwestern France, successor to the Duchy of Gascony, held by the English for three centuries until they lost nearly all their French territory there after 1453.

northumbria.name: Northumbria
northumbria.summary: An early medieval English kingdom existing from 654 to 1066 AD, spanning modern northern England and southern Scotland at its height.

harrying-of-the-north.name: Harrying of the North
harrying-of-the-north.summary: William the Conqueror's 1069–1070 campaigns to crush rebellion in northern England by laying waste to the land, causing famine so severe that Domesday Book records suggest up to 75% of the population died or fled; some scholars call it a genocide.

battle-of-patay.name: Battle of Patay
battle-of-patay.summary: An 18 June 1429 Hundred Years' War battle in which French cavalry crushed an English army, capturing nearly all its senior commanders and dealing a severe blow to English hopes in France.

house-of-plantagenet.name: Plantagenet dynasty
house-of-plantagenet.summary: A royal house from Anjou, France, that held the English throne from 1154 to 1485, overseeing changes such as Magna Carta and the rise of Middle English in government.

henry-vi-of-england.name: Henry VI of England
henry-vi-of-england.summary: King of England from 1422 to 1461 and 1470 to 1471, crowned king of France as a child, whose mental incapacity from 1453 helped trigger the Wars of the Roses.

henry-i-of-england.name: Henry I of England
henry-i-of-england.summary: King of England from 1100 to 1135, fourth son of William the Conqueror, who defeated his brother Robert at the Battle of Tinchebray in 1106.

robert-curthose.name: Robert Curthose
robert-curthose.summary: Eldest son of William the Conqueror and Duke of Normandy (1087-1106); twice an unsuccessful claimant to the English throne, he mortgaged Normandy for the First Crusade and was later defeated and imprisoned for life by his brother Henry I.

battle-of-tinchebray.name: Battle of Tinchebray
battle-of-tinchebray.summary: A battle fought on 28 September 1106 in Normandy in which King Henry I of England defeated and captured his brother Robert Curthose, Duke of Normandy, who remained imprisoned until his death in 1134.

battle-of-br-mule.name: Battle of Brémule
battle-of-br-mule.summary: A battle fought on 20 August 1119 in which Henry I of England defeated Louis VI of France, repelling a French invasion of Normandy and crippling a baronial rebellion.

louis-vi-of-france.name: Louis VI of France
louis-vi-of-france.summary: King of the Franks from 1108 to 1137, nicknamed 'the Fat,' who centralized royal power and fought robber barons and Henry I of England.

crusade-cycle.name: Old French Crusade cycle
crusade-cycle.summary: A medieval French literary cycle of chansons de geste, or heroic verse tales, about the First Crusade and its aftermath.

occitania.name: Occitania
occitania.summary: The historical region of southern Europe, mainly southern France plus parts of Spain, Monaco and Italy, where the Occitan language was traditionally spoken.

charles-homer-haskins.name: Charles Homer Haskins
charles-homer-haskins.summary: American medievalist historian (1870–1937) at Harvard and advisor to President Woodrow Wilson, widely seen as the first academic medieval historian in the United States.

renaissance-of-the-12th-century.name: Renaissance of the 12th century
renaissance-of-the-12th-century.summary: A period of intellectual, social and economic revival in 12th-century Western Europe, spurred by renewed contact with Islamic scholarship, paving the way for the later Italian Renaissance.

matter-of-britain.name: Matter of Britain
matter-of-britain.summary: The body of medieval legend and literature about Great Britain and Brittany, centred on King Arthur, that flourished from the 12th to 16th centuries.

king-arthur.name: King Arthur
king-arthur.summary: A legendary king of Britain and central figure of medieval literature, first portrayed in early Welsh sources fighting the Anglo-Saxons; most historians doubt he was a real person.

geoffrey-chaucer.name: Geoffrey Chaucer
geoffrey-chaucer.summary: An English poet (c. 1343-1400) best known for The Canterbury Tales, called the "father of English literature" for helping legitimize Middle English as a literary language.

the-canterbury-tales.name: The Canterbury Tales
the-canterbury-tales.summary: A collection of 24 stories in Middle English written by Geoffrey Chaucer between 1387 and 1400, framed as a storytelling contest among pilgrims travelling to Canterbury, and credited with helping popularize English as a literary language.

middle-english.name: Middle English
middle-english.summary: The form of the English language spoken from the Norman Conquest of 1066 to the late 15th century, shaped by Anglo-Norman French and Old Norse.

the-king-of-tars.name: The King of Tars
the-king-of-tars.summary: A medieval English chivalric romance from around 1330, strongly religious in tone and blending hagiography, political drama and miracle tale.

song-of-roland.name: Song of Roland
song-of-roland.summary: An 11th-century French epic poem about the Frankish leader Roland's death at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778, and the oldest surviving major work of French literature.

saracen.name: Saracen
saracen.summary: A medieval European term originally for Arabian tribes that widened to mean Muslims generally, becoming the standard word for people and things of the Muslim world by the Crusades.

jean-bodel.name: Jean Bodel
jean-bodel.summary: An Old French poet, also spelled Jehan Bodel, who lived in Arras around 1165 to 1210 and wrote chansons de geste and fabliaux.

matter-of-france.name: Matter of France
matter-of-france.summary: Also called the Carolingian cycle, a body of medieval legend about Charlemagne and his knights, one of three great story cycles of medieval literature.

charlemagne.name: Charlemagne
charlemagne.summary: King of the Franks from 768 and emperor of the Carolingian Empire from 800, who united most of Western and Central Europe and was the first recognised western emperor since Rome's fall.

matter-of-rome.name: Matter of Rome
matter-of-rome.summary: A medieval literary cycle drawing on Greek and Roman mythology and history, including tales of Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar and the Trojan War.

geoffrey-of-monmouth.name: Geoffrey of Monmouth
geoffrey-of-monmouth.summary: A Christian cleric from Wales (c. 1095–c. 1155) whose chronicle, the History of the Kings of Britain, popularised tales of King Arthur though later judged historically unreliable.

wace.name: Wace
wace.summary: A 12th-century Norman poet, born in Jersey and raised in Normandy, who ended his career as a Canon of Bayeux.

mabinogion.name: Mabinogion
mabinogion.summary: Collection of the earliest Welsh prose stories, compiled in Middle Welsh in the 12th to 13th centuries from older oral traditions, including early Arthurian tales.

layamon-s-brut.name: Layamon's Brut
layamon-s-brut.summary: A Middle English poem, about 1190 to 1215, retelling the legendary history of Britain; the first history written in English since the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

anglo-saxon-chronicle.name: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
anglo-saxon-chronicle.summary: A set of Old English annals on Anglo-Saxon history, first compiled in the late 800s under King Alfred the Great and copied and updated at English monasteries until 1154; its oldest surviving manuscript, held at Cambridge, is called the Parker Chronicle.

ormulum.name: The Ormulum
ormulum.summary: A 12th-century work of biblical exegesis in nearly 19,000 lines of early Middle English verse, valued for its unique spelling system that preserves details of English pronunciation after the Norman Conquest.

anglo-norman-language.name: Anglo-Norman
anglo-norman-language.summary: A dialect of Old Norman French used in England, and to a lesser degree elsewhere in Britain and Ireland, during the Anglo-Norman period.

roman-de-fauvel.name: Roman de Fauvel
roman-de-fauvel.summary: A 14th-century French satirical verse romance featuring a horse named Fauvel that mocks hypocrisy and corruption in the church and nobility, notable for its many interpolated musical pieces.

philippe-de-vitry.name: Philippe de Vitry
philippe-de-vitry.summary: French composer-poet, bishop and music theorist (1291–1361) in the ars nova style, widely acknowledged as a leading musician of his day.

ars-nova.name: Ars nova
ars-nova.summary: A musical style that flourished in France during the Late Middle Ages, roughly from the 1310s to the death of composer Guillaume de Machaut in 1377.

antoine-de-la-sale.name: Antoine de la Sale
antoine-de-la-sale.summary: French courtier, educator and writer (1385/86–1460/61) who took part in military campaigns in his youth before writing works including Little John of Saintré in 1456.

thomas-malory.name: Thomas Malory
thomas-malory.summary: An English writer, likely a knight imprisoned during the Wars of the Roses, who compiled Le Morte d'Arthur, the classic English telling of the Arthurian legend, published in 1485.

le-morte-d-arthur.name: Le Morte d'Arthur
le-morte-d-arthur.summary: A 15th-century Middle English prose compilation of Arthurian legends by Sir Thomas Malory, completed around 1470 and first printed in 1485.

three-field-system.name: Three-field system
three-field-system.summary: A medieval crop rotation method dividing farmland into three fields, rotating grain, legumes and fallow land each year, which raised agricultural yields across Europe.

william-caxton.name: William Caxton
william-caxton.summary: English merchant, diplomat and writer (c. 1422–c. 1491) believed to have introduced the first printing press to England in 1476, becoming the country's first retailer of printed books.

wynkyn-de-worde.name: Wynkyn de Worde
wynkyn-de-worde.summary: Printer and publisher in London, died 1534, who worked with William Caxton and is credited as the first to popularize printing press products in England.

domesday-book.name: Domesday Book
domesday-book.summary: Manuscript record of a great survey of England and parts of Wales, believed completed in 1086 for William the Conqueror, listing landholdings, resources and their value.

poleyn.name: Poleyn
poleyn.summary: A piece of medieval and Renaissance plate armor protecting the knee, first appearing around 1230 and used until firearms made it obsolete around 1650.

couter.name: Couter
couter.summary: A piece of plate armour protecting the elbow, popular from the 1320s onward, which developed from a simple curved plate into an articulated joint.

blast-furnace.name: blast furnace
blast-furnace.summary: A furnace for smelting metal, chiefly iron ore into pig iron, using a continuous blast of hot air fed in through pipes as fuel and ore are added from the top.

matthew-paris.name: Matthew Paris
matthew-paris.summary: English Benedictine monk and chronicler (c. 1200–1259) at St Albans Abbey, whose illustrated Chronica Majora is a key source for mid-13th-century Europe.

third-council-of-the-lateran.name: Third Lateran Council
third-council-of-the-lateran.summary: An ecumenical council held in Rome in March 1179, presided over by Pope Alexander III with 302 bishops attending; the Catholic Church counts it as the eleventh such council.

fourth-council-of-the-lateran.name: Fourth Lateran Council
fourth-council-of-the-lateran.summary: A major 1215 Catholic Church council under Pope Innocent III that issued sweeping decrees on confession, the treatment of Jews and heretics, and church organization.

cnut.name: Cnut
cnut.summary: King of England from 1016, Denmark from 1018, and Norway from 1028 until his death in 1035, ruling the three kingdoms together as the North Sea Empire.

north-sea-empire.name: North Sea Empire
north-sea-empire.summary: Personal union of England, Denmark and Norway under Norse kings for most of 1013 to 1042; at its height under Cnut the Great it was the most powerful realm in western Europe after the Holy Roman Empire.

charles-iv-of-france.name: Charles IV of France
charles-iv-of-france.summary: King of France and Navarre from 1322 to 1328, the last king of the direct line of the House of Capet, whose death without a male heir ended that line.

capetian-dynasty.name: Capetian dynasty
capetian-dynasty.summary: A royal dynasty of Frankish origin founded by Hugh Capet in 987, whose male line and later Valois and Bourbon branches ruled France almost continuously into the 19th century.

salic-law.name: Salic law
salic-law.summary: A Frankish legal code compiled around 500 AD under King Clovis, best known for excluding women from inheriting thrones, fiefs and property, which shaped later European law.

philip-vi-of-france.name: Philip VI of France
philip-vi-of-france.summary: First king of France from the House of Valois, reigning 1328–1350, whose disputed succession with Edward III of England helped spark the Hundred Years' War.

edward-iii.name: Edward III
edward-iii.summary: King of England from 1327 to 1377 whose fifty-year reign, one of the longest in English history, saw him start the Hundred Years' War and oversee the growth of Parliament.

angevin-empire.name: Angevin Empire
angevin-empire.summary: The territories held by the House of Plantagenet in the 12th and 13th centuries, covering roughly all of England, half of France, and parts of Ireland and Wales, established by Henry II.

philip-ii-of-france.name: Philip II of France
philip-ii-of-france.summary: King of France from 1180 to 1223 who defeated a rival coalition at the Battle of Bouvines in 1214 and was the first monarch to style himself 'King of France.'

edward-ii.name: Edward II
edward-ii.summary: King of England from 1307 to 1327, son of Edward I, whose close relationship with favourite Piers Gaveston provoked baronial unrest and years of armed conflict before his deposition.

battle-of-bannockburn.name: Battle of Bannockburn
battle-of-bannockburn.summary: A decisive battle fought on 23-24 June 1314, in which Robert the Bruce's Scottish army defeated King Edward II of England, a major turning point in the First War of Scottish Independence.

henry-v-of-england.name: Henry V of England
henry-v-of-england.summary: King of England from 1413 to 1422 whose victory at Agincourt in 1415 and conquest of Normandy led to his recognition as heir to the French throne.

armagnac-burgundian-civil-war.name: Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War
armagnac-burgundian-civil-war.summary: Conflict from 1407 to 1435 between the House of Orléans (Armagnac faction) and the House of Burgundy (Burgundian faction), rival branches of the French royal family, overlapping with the Hundred Years' War.

treaty-of-troyes.name: Treaty of Troyes
treaty-of-troyes.summary: 1420 agreement that Henry V of England and his heirs would inherit the French throne on the death of Charles VI.

joan-of-arc.name: Joan of Arc
joan-of-arc.summary: French peasant girl turned military leader (c. 1412–1431) who, claiming divine guidance, relieved the siege of Orléans and secured Charles VII's coronation.

john-of-lancaster-duke-of-bedford.name: Duke of Bedford
john-of-lancaster-duke-of-bedford.summary: English prince and general (1389–1435), son of Henry IV, who commanded England's armies in France as regent for young Henry VI during the Hundred Years' War.
john-of-lancaster-duke-of-bedford.source_title: John of Lancaster, Duke of Bedford

humphrey-duke-of-gloucester.name: Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester
humphrey-duke-of-gloucester.summary: An English prince, soldier and literary patron (1390-1447), youngest son of Henry IV, who fought in the Hundred Years' War and served as Lord Protector during Henry VI's minority.

henry-beaufort.name: Henry Beaufort
henry-beaufort.summary: English bishop, cardinal, and statesman (c. 1375 to 1447) of the royal House of Plantagenet, who served three times as Lord Chancellor.

philip-the-good.name: Philip the Good
philip-the-good.summary: Duke of Burgundy from 1419 to 1467, under whom the Burgundian State reached its height of prosperity, and who had Joan of Arc ransomed to the English after her capture.

guyenne.name: Guyenne
guyenne.summary: An old French province roughly matching the Roman province of Aquitania Secunda, in the region around Bordeaux.

william-ii-of-england.name: William Rufus
william-ii-of-england.summary: King of England from 1087 to 1100, third son of William the Conqueror, nicknamed 'Rufus' for his ruddy appearance or red hair; died after being struck by an arrow while hunting, amid suspicions of murder.

odo-of-bayeux.name: Odo of Bayeux
odo-of-bayeux.summary: Norman bishop of Bayeux and Earl of Kent, half-brother of William the Conqueror, who likely commissioned the Bayeux Tapestry and served as William's chief administrator in England.

county-of-artois.name: County of Artois
county-of-artois.summary: A historic province of northern France near the Belgian border, held by the Dukes of Burgundy from 1384 and later a state of the Holy Roman Empire from 1493.

county-of-anjou.name: County of Anjou
county-of-anjou.summary: A historic French county centered on Angers whose 12th-century count Geoffrey founded the nucleus of the Angevin Empire; it was raised into a duchy in 1360 and absorbed into the French crown in 1482.

treaty-of-picquigny.name: Treaty of Picquigny
treaty-of-picquigny.summary: 1475 peace treaty between England and France in which Edward IV agreed not to pursue his claim to the French throne, formally ending the Hundred Years' War.

edward-iv.name: Edward IV
edward-iv.summary: King of England (1461-1483, with a brief interruption) and central Yorkist figure in the Wars of the Roses, who twice took the throne from the Lancastrian Henry VI.

house-of-valois.name: House of Valois
house-of-valois.summary: A branch of the Capetian dynasty that held the French throne from 1328 to 1589, descended from Charles, Count of Valois, until succeeded by the House of Bourbon.

joan-ii-of-navarre.name: Joan II of Navarre
joan-ii-of-navarre.summary: Queen of Navarre from 1328 to 1349, whose claim to the French throne was blocked by Salic Law despite her father's declaration of her legitimacy.

merovingian-dynasty.name: Merovingian dynasty
merovingian-dynasty.summary: The ruling family of the Franks from the mid-5th century until 751, who united the Franks and conquered much of Gaul; known for wearing their hair long as a mark of royal legitimacy.

term-logic.name: Term logic
term-logic.summary: Also called traditional or syllogistic logic, this approach to formal reasoning began with Aristotle and dominated logic in Europe and the Islamic world until the late 19th century.

scholasticism.name: Scholasticism
scholasticism.summary: Medieval European method of philosophical and theological study, dominant from about 1100 to 1700, using rigorous logical debate to reconcile Aristotle's philosophy with Christian theology.

john-scotus-eriugena.name: John Scotus Eriugena
john-scotus-eriugena.summary: Irish Neoplatonist philosopher, theologian and poet (c.800–877), called the most original philosopher of the Carolingian era, known for his work Periphyseon.

lanfranc.name: Lanfranc
lanfranc.summary: An Italian-born churchman and scholar (c. 1005/10-1089) who became a Benedictine monk in Normandy and later Archbishop of Canterbury under William the Conqueror, regarded as his era's greatest theologian.

anselm-of-canterbury.name: Anselm of Canterbury
anselm-of-canterbury.summary: Benedictine abbot, philosopher and theologian who served as Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093 to 1109; credited as originator of the ontological argument for God's existence.

peter-abelard.name: Peter Abelard
peter-abelard.summary: A 12th-century French philosopher, logician and theologian famed for his love affair with his student Héloïse, and for his influential ideas on logic, ethics and Church doctrine.

ontological-argument.name: Ontological argument
ontological-argument.summary: Type of philosophical argument for God's existence based purely on reasoning about being, first proposed in the West by Anselm of Canterbury in 1078.

aosta.name: Aosta
aosta.summary: The capital of Italy's Aosta Valley region in the Alps, near the entrances to the Mont Blanc and Great St Bernard tunnels.

bec-abbey.name: Bec Abbey
bec-abbey.summary: A Benedictine abbey in Normandy, France, the most influential monastery of the 12th-century Anglo-Norman kingdom, where Anselm studied under Lanfranc.

william-of-moerbeke.name: William of Moerbeke
william-of-moerbeke.summary: William of Moerbeke: 13th-century translator who rendered Greek philosophical, medical and scientific texts into Latin; his translations were influential and are still respected by modern scholars.

john-wycliffe.name: John Wycliffe
john-wycliffe.summary: English scholastic philosopher, Christian reformer and Oxford theology professor (c. 1328–1384) whose dissident ideas are considered an important predecessor to Protestantism.

satisfaction-theory-of-atonement.name: Satisfaction theory of atonement
satisfaction-theory-of-atonement.summary: A Christian theory, developed by Anselm of Canterbury, holding that Jesus's obedience 'satisfied' the demands of divine justice for human disobedience; it influenced later theologians such as John Calvin.

on-the-soul.name: De Anima
on-the-soul.summary: Aristotle's treatise, written around 350 BC, classifying the souls of living things by their capacities for nourishment, sense-perception, and intellect.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

gerard-of-siena.name: Gerard of Siena
gerard-of-siena.summary: Tuscan scholar (c. 1295-1336) who studied under Giles of Rome at the University of Paris, opposed usury, and lectured on Peter Lombard's Sentences.

giles-of-rome.name: Giles of Rome
giles-of-rome.summary: Italian medieval philosopher and Scholastic theologian (c. 1243–1316), an Augustinian friar who served as prior general and Archbishop of Bourges, known for works on Aristotle and Christian rule.

peter-lombard.name: Peter Lombard
peter-lombard.summary: Italian scholastic theologian and Bishop of Paris (c. 1096–1160), author of the Sentences, the standard medieval theology textbook.

sentences.name: Sentences
sentences.summary: A compendium of Christian theology written by Peter Lombard around 1150, the most important religious textbook of the Middle Ages.

cistercians.name: Cistercians
cistercians.summary: A Catholic monastic order founded in 1098 near Cîteaux, France, known for austere living, manual labor and major contributions to architecture and culture.

rievaulx-abbey.name: Rievaulx Abbey
rievaulx-abbey.summary: A Cistercian abbey in North Yorkshire, England, one of the great English monasteries until it was seized in 1538 under Henry VIII; its ruins are now a tourist attraction.

fountains-abbey.name: Fountains Abbey
fountains-abbey.summary: A ruined Cistercian monastery near Ripon, England, founded in 1132, once one of the wealthiest monasteries before its 1539 dissolution.

second-crusade.name: Second Crusade
second-crusade.summary: A campaign of 1147 to 1149 launched after the fall of the Crusader County of Edessa, in which European armies under Louis VII and Conrad III were defeated in Anatolia before an unsuccessful attack on Damascus.

third-crusade.name: Third Crusade
third-crusade.summary: A 1189–1192 campaign led by the kings of France and England and the Holy Roman Emperor to retake the Holy Land after Saladin's 1187 capture of Jerusalem; it recovered Acre and Jaffa but not Jerusalem itself.

fifth-crusade.name: Fifth Crusade
fifth-crusade.summary: A 1217-1221 campaign by Western Europeans to retake Jerusalem by first conquering Egypt's Ayyubid Sultanate, ending after early success at Damietta turned to failure near Cairo.

henry-iii-of-england.name: Henry III of England
henry-iii-of-england.summary: King of England, Lord of Ireland and Duke of Aquitaine from 1216 until his death in 1272; he came to the throne at age nine and agreed to the Great Charter limiting royal power in 1225.
